nary_nodes.label: World Cup 2026 hydration breaks
evidence: It's one reason why players at the World Cup 2026 in the US, Canada and Mexico are being given additional, but controversial hydration breaks 22 minutes into each half.
nary_nodes.type_justification: World Cup 2026 hydration breaks is a sports event.

nary_nodes.label: Record temperatures this summer
evidence: And with record temperatures on their way this summer thanks to a powerful El Niño weather pattern, it's likely to be a tough time to exercise.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A period of abnormally hot weather, often lasting several days or weeks.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; record temperatures is a weather event.

nary_nodes.label: Research warns of premature deaths
evidence: García-Witulski and colleagues have recently warned in new research that rising temperatures due to climate change could lead to people moving less in the heat and consequentially result in an estimated 470,000 to 700,000 premature deaths per year by 2050.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A result or conclusion from research, such as a warning of premature deaths.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; research warning is a finding, not a user interaction.

nary_nodes.label: Body cools during exercise
evidence: As you work out, your muscles contract and generate heat. Your body then tries to cool itself by sweating and diverting blood towards the skin.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A biological function or activity in a living organism, such as heat acclimatisation or blood flow.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; these are physiological processes, not user interactions.

nary_nodes.label: Blood robbed from muscles
evidence: But that creates a trade-off as the same blood is also needed to supply oxygen to your muscles, says Ollie Jay from the University of Sydney. "Your skin is basically robbing blood from your muscles, so you can't deliver as much oxygen to them."
nary_nodes.type_definition: A biological function or activity in a living organism, such as heat acclimatisation or blood flow.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; these are physiological processes, not user interactions.

nary_nodes.label: Fatigue and heart strain
evidence: In hot conditions, can very quickly lead to fatigue as your body struggles to get enough oxygen to your muscles, but it can also put extra strain on your heart as it tries to keep up with the demand.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A result of physiological processes, such as fatigue and heart strain.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; fatigue and heart strain are effects, not user interactions.

nary_nodes.label: Exercise when cooler
evidence: The single most impactful change most people can make is to exercise when it is cooler, such as in the morning or evening, if this is possible.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A suggestion or advice for action, such as exercising when cooler.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; these are recommendations, not user interactions or sales events.

nary_nodes.label: Choose shaded areas
evidence: You could also pick times when the area where you like to exercise is in the shade as opposed to the full glare of the Sun. "That difference can be as much as 12-15C (22-27F) higher than the shaded air temperature," says Ollie Jay, director of the Heat and Health Research Centre at the University of Sydney.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A suggestion or advice for action, such as exercising when cooler.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; these are recommendations, not user interactions or sales events.

nary_nodes.label: Consider humidity and wind
evidence: Humidity matters too. Your body's primary way of losing heat is through sweat evaporating from the skin, which helps to lower your body temperature. But in humid conditions, that process is affected as the evaporation that cools your body reduces. Wind speed also plays a role, which is why running in enclosed spaces with little airflow makes heat stress a bigger risk.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A suggestion or advice for action, such as exercising when cooler.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; these are recommendations, not user interactions or sales events.

nary_nodes.label: Shorten exercise and add breaks
evidence: On days when you can't avoid the heat, you might consider exercising for shorter periods of time as well as adding in more breaks.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A suggestion or advice for action, such as exercising when cooler.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; these are recommendations, not user interactions or sales events.

nary_nodes.label: Cool down in breaks
evidence: Rebecca Stearns, a kinesiologist at the Korey Stringer Institute at the University of Connecticut says that while taking breaks from exercise, find a cooler environment where possible. "If you can get inside an air-conditioned environment, or even just shade with cold water and a fan, take time to actually start to cool down," she says.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A suggestion or advice for action, such as exercising when cooler.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; these are recommendations, not user interactions or sales events.

nary_nodes.label: Heat tool developed
evidence: (For those who want to check their potential heat stress risk, Jay and colleagues at the University of Sydney have developed a free heat tool covering over 40 sports that draws on your local weather data.)
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event of developing or advancing technology or applications.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; development is a process, not a publication event.

nary_nodes.label: Use immersion cooling
evidence: Immersion cooling can be a better way to cool down. This is where you submerge parts of the body (such as the hands and forearms) in cold water. Alternatively, you can pour water over yourself.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A suggestion or advice for action, such as exercising when cooler.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; these are recommendations, not user interactions or sales events.

nary_nodes.label: Apply water to skin
evidence: "If you take water and apply it to the skin surface, and then that water evaporates, that's actually doing the job of sweating without having to sweat," says Jay. That then means your body can direct more blood to your muscles to deliver oxygen.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A suggestion or advice for action, such as exercising when cooler.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; these are recommendations, not user interactions or sales events.

nary_nodes.label: Use cold wet towel
evidence: Similarly, a cold wet towel frequently rotated over your arms, legs and torso also helps cool you down, says Stearns.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A suggestion or advice for action, such as exercising when cooler.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; these are recommendations, not user interactions or sales events.

nary_nodes.label: Pre-cool before exercise
evidence: Pre-cooling before you head out is also helpful. Research shows that reducing body temperature before exercise gives you a greater heat buffer before conditions become dangerous. "Slightly lowering your body temperature before you go into the heat will give you a greater amount of time before it becomes dangerous," Stearns says.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A suggestion or advice for action, such as exercising when cooler.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; these are recommendations, not user interactions or sales events.

nary_nodes.label: Consume ice slurry
evidence: This can also be done by consuming ice slurry (icy water), which has been found to cool the body and improve exercise performance.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A suggestion or advice for action, such as exercising when cooler.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; these are recommendations, not user interactions or sales events.

nary_nodes.label: Heat acclimatisation
evidence: Gradually building up the amount of exercise you do in hot weather will allow your body get used to it, a process called heat acclimatisation.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A series of actions or steps, such as heat acclimatisation.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; heat acclimatisation is a process, not an event type.

nary_nodes.label: Adaptations after 7-14 days
evidence: Generally, says Stearns, after seven to 14 days of regularly exercising in the heat your core temperature at rest drops, your sweat rate rises and your blood plasma volume increases. "You have this huge demand for blood flow. And blood is ultimately what's going to be able to supply and support all of these physiological functions in the heat," she says.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A change in the body in response to environmental stress, such as adaptations after 7-14 days.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; adaptations are physiological changes, not user interactions.

nary_nodes.label: Adaptations are transient
evidence: But this response is "transient", says Jay. "If you don't use it, you'll lose it… If you don't expose yourself to the heat, then those adaptations that you've primed will disappear."
nary_nodes.type_definition: A biological function or activity in a living organism, such as heat acclimatisation or blood flow.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; these are physiological processes, not user interactions.

nary_nodes.label: Heat exhaustion becoming common
evidence: While fatalities from exercising in the heat are relatively rare, heat exhaustion is becoming more common.
nary_nodes.type_definition: The possibility of harm or loss, such as heat exhaustion becoming common.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; risk is a state, not a sports event or user interaction.

nary_nodes.label: Elite athletes at higher risk
evidence: Elite athletes can be at a higher risk of heatstroke than recreational exercisers because they are already used to pushing themselves "past their biological limits", says Stearns. This could be dangerous as the intensity of the exercise is the primary driver of rising internal body temperature.
nary_nodes.type_definition: The possibility of harm or loss, such as heat exhaustion becoming common.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; risk is a state, not a sports event or user interaction.

nary_nodes.label: Listen to your body
evidence: She therefore advises that "listening to your body and deliberately backing off the pace is your primary line of defence".
nary_nodes.type_definition: A suggestion or advice for action, such as exercising when cooler.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; these are recommendations, not user interactions or sales events.

nary_nodes.label: Stop if symptoms appear
evidence: Heat related illness is still a risk so signs to look out for include dizziness, nausea, fatigue and palpitations. If any of these appear, stop immediately and cool down.
nary_nodes.type_definition: A suggestion or advice for action, such as exercising when cooler.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org class fits; these are recommendations, not user interactions or sales events.

nary_nodes.label: Heat makes exercise harder
evidence: "Walking, cycling, exercising outdoors and even daily routines like commuting on foot become more physically demanding and less comfortable when temperatures are high," says Christian García-Witulski, an environmental lifestyle epidemiologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Argentina.

nary_nodes.label: Reduced activity harms health
evidence: But if we reduce our physical activity each time it feels too hot to exercise outside, it can contribute to long-term health risks.

nary_nodes.label: Shorter walks safer
evidence: "Sometimes a shorter walk in the morning, or some light indoor movement, is safer and more realistic than trying to stick rigidly to the same routine," says García-Witulski. "Hotter conditions create more thermal strain. People tire more easily, sweat more, may feel dizzy or uncomfortable, often sleep worse and daily movement simply becomes less appealing and, in some cases, less safe."

nary_nodes.label: Ice packs low cooling rate
evidence: But Stearns says that while ice packs feel cold to the skin they actually have a surprisingly low cooling rate because they tend to only cover a small part of the skin.

nary_nodes.label: Exercise not separate from climate
evidence: "I think the bigger message is that we should stop thinking of physical activity as something completely separate from climate," says García-Witulski. "As heatwaves become more common, people will increasingly need to adapt not just whether they move, but when, where, and how they do it," he adds.
